title: Routing
summary: How packets find their path across networks — from routing tables and static routes to dynamic algorithms and the protocols that power the internet.

blocks.markdown:
**Routing** is how the internet decides the path a packet takes from source to destination across multiple networks.

- The **network layer** (Layer 3) handles host-to-host delivery across different networks.
- Every router reads the packet's destination IP and decides: which interface should this leave on?
- Two core jobs: **forwarding** (moving one packet) and **routing** (building the map).
- Protocols like RIP, OSPF, and BGP automate map-building across the internet.

The **network layer** (Layer 3 in OSI) is responsible for delivering packets from a source host to a destination host, even when they sit on completely different networks.

- Layer 2 (data link) only moves frames between directly connected devices on the same network segment.
- Layer 3 adds the logic to hop **across** routers and networks.
- It assigns **logical addresses** (IP addresses) that identify hosts globally.

See [osi-tcpip-models](osi-tcpip-models) and [ipv4-addressing](ipv4-addressing) for context.

These two terms sound alike but describe different timescales.

- **Forwarding** — when a packet arrives, look up the destination in the routing table and send it out the right interface. Happens in nanoseconds, per packet.
- **Routing** — building and updating the routing table itself. Happens in the background, over seconds to minutes.

Think of routing as drawing the map; forwarding as following it.

A **routing table** is the lookup map inside every router (and every OS). Each row answers: "for packets destined to this network, send them here."

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Destination network | The target IP prefix (e.g. 10.1.0.0/24) |
| Next hop | IP of the next router to send to |
| Interface | Local port the packet leaves on |

The router picks the **longest-matching prefix** when multiple rows match.

blocks.subTitle: Longest-prefix match
blocks.markdown:
When multiple routing table rows match a destination, the router always picks the **most specific** one — the one with the longest prefix mask.

- Row A: 10.0.0.0/8 → Router X
- Row B: 10.1.0.0/16 → Router Y

A packet for 10.1.2.3 matches both, but /16 is longer, so it goes to Router Y. This is called **longest-prefix match** and is how routing scales to billions of addresses.

Each router is just one hop on a chain — the packet hops until it reaches the destination network.

Each router has a small routing table bubble showing next-hop arrows. Clean, blue-grey palette, generous whitespace. >>>

- Source sends packet to its **default gateway** (R1).
- Each router checks destination IP → picks next hop → forwards.
- Process repeats until the packet arrives at the destination network.

A **default gateway** is the router an end host sends all non-local traffic to. It's the first hop out of the local network.

- If a destination IP is outside the local subnet, the host has no direct route — it hands the packet to the default gateway.
- The default gateway is the "exit door" for traffic leaving the local network.
- Configured on every device (phone, laptop, server) — usually the local router's IP.

Routing tables can be built by hand or automatically.

| | Static | Dynamic |
|---|---|---|
| Set by | Admin, manually | Routing protocol |
| Adapts to failure | No | Yes |
| CPU/bandwidth cost | None | Small overhead |

- **Static** — fixed routes, no overhead, but fragile; no auto-recovery.
- **Dynamic** — routers exchange info and recompute paths; adapts when links fail.

Small, stable networks use static. Anything bigger uses dynamic.

blocks.subTitle: Distance-vector
blocks.markdown:
**Distance-vector** algorithms work by sharing routing tables with neighbors.

- Each router tells neighbors: "I can reach network X in N hops."
- Neighbors update their own tables based on what they hear.
- Over time, all routers converge on correct paths — but convergence can be slow after a failure.
- Example protocol: **RIP** (Routing Information Protocol), max 15 hops.

Weakness: routers only know their neighbors' view, not the whole network topology.

blocks.subTitle: Link-state
blocks.markdown:
**Link-state** algorithms give every router a full map of the network.

- Each router floods its link costs to all other routers.
- Every router independently runs **Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm** to find the best routes.
- Converges faster than distance-vector; no counting-to-infinity.
- Example protocol: **OSPF** (Open Shortest Path First).

Trade-off: more memory and CPU, but much better at scale and recovery speed.

blocks.subTitle: Distance-vector vs link-state
blocks.markdown:
| | Distance-vector | Link-state |
|---|---|---|
| Knowledge | Neighbor's table | Full topology map |
| Algorithm | Bellman-Ford | Dijkstra |
| Convergence | Slow | Fast |
| Example | RIP | OSPF |

- Distance-vector: simpler, lower overhead, slower to recover.
- Link-state: more state, faster recovery, used in real enterprise networks.

Three protocols you'll see in interviews and real systems.

- **RIP** (Routing Information Protocol) — distance-vector, 15-hop limit, slow convergence. Simple but outdated for large networks.
- **OSPF** (Open Shortest Path First) — link-state, fast convergence, widely used inside enterprise and ISP networks.
- **BGP** (Border Gateway Protocol) — the protocol that connects different organizations (autonomous systems) on the internet. It is the routing glue of the public internet.

See [bgp-internet-routing](bgp-internet-routing) for BGP deep dive.

**NAT (Network Address Translation)** lets many devices share one public IP address. It sits at the border between a private network and the internet.

- Private addresses (10.x, 192.168.x) are not routable on the internet.
- The NAT router rewrites the source IP on outgoing packets to its own public IP, then tracks which internal host each reply belongs to.
- This is why your home network has one public IP but dozens of devices.

Full detail in [nat-firewalls](nat-firewalls).

blocks.subTitle: Forwarding vs routing
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between forwarding and routing?**

**Forwarding** is the per-packet data-plane action: look up the destination in the table and send the packet out the right interface. **Routing** is the control-plane process that builds and maintains that table. Routing happens in the background; forwarding happens on the fast path for every packet.

blocks.subTitle: Distance-vector vs link-state
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Distance-vector vs link-state — what's the key trade-off?**

Distance-vector routers share tables only with neighbors and can be slow to converge after a failure (counting-to-infinity problem). Link-state routers flood the full topology to everyone and run Dijkstra independently, so convergence is fast. OSPF (link-state) is used in real networks; RIP (distance-vector) is mostly a teaching protocol now.

blocks.subTitle: What is a default gateway
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is a default gateway and why does every host need one?**

It's the router an end host forwards all off-subnet traffic to — the "exit door." A host only knows how to reach devices on its own subnet directly; for everything else it hands the packet to the default gateway, which then routes it onward.
